stages.name: Basics
body: Computers find each other by IP address, but people remember names. DNS, the Domain Name System, is the service that turns a name like www.example.com into the address a computer can actually connect to. It does this before almost every connection on the internet, which is why it has to be fast and hard to break.

DNS is not one big list kept in one place. The names form a tree. At the top is the root, then top-level domains such as com or uk, then the names under them, and so on. Each piece between the dots is a label, and reading the labels from left to right up to the root gives the full domain name [[bind-arm]].

The specification describes DNS as three parts working together: the tree of names and the data attached to them, the name servers that hold that data, and the resolvers that go and fetch it for whoever is asking [[rfc1034]]. Every later idea on this page is one of those three parts doing its job.

terms.definition: A name in the DNS tree, written as labels separated by dots, such as www.example.com.
One piece of a domain name between dots, such as www, example or com.
One piece of data attached to a name, such as the address for www.example.com.
A server that holds DNS data for part of the tree and answers questions about it.
A program that asks name servers on someone's behalf and returns the answer.

reading.what: How the tree of names is organized, from the root to top-level and second-level domains.

stages.name: How it works
body: Your device does not search the internet itself. A small piece of software on it, the stub resolver, sends the question to a recursive resolver, often run by your internet provider or your network. The recursive resolver does the work of finding the answer and hands it back [[bind-arm]].

If the recursive resolver has no saved copy, it starts at the top. It asks a root server, which does not know the final answer but replies with a referral: the servers responsible for the top-level domain. It asks one of those, gets another referral to the servers for the domain itself, and finally asks those, which are authoritative and give the real answer [[bind-arm]]. The root is served under 13 named authorities, made up of hundreds of servers around the world [[iana-root]].

Each part of the tree whose data is managed together is a zone, and a parent zone delegates a child zone to the child's own name servers. By convention a zone has at least two name servers, so one failure does not take its names offline [[cs168]].

Answers come as resource records of different types: an address record for IPv4 or IPv6, a record naming a zone's name servers, an alias pointing one name at another, a record saying where mail for a domain should go, and more [[rfc1035]]. Every record carries a time to live, which tells resolvers how long they may keep reusing a copy before asking again.

There are hard limits built into names: each label is at most 63 octets and a whole name at most 255 octets [[rfc1035]]. Queries usually travel over UDP on port 53, and TCP or TLS can also be used in parts of the network [[bind-arm]].

terms.definition: The small resolver on your device that passes questions to a recursive resolver.
A resolver that does the whole lookup for you, following referrals and caching what it learns.
A name server for the very top of the tree; it refers resolvers to the top-level domains.
The last label in a name, such as com or uk, with its own name servers.
A name server that holds the real data for a zone, rather than a cached copy.
A reply that does not answer the question but names the servers that know more.
A part of the tree managed together; delegation hands a child zone to its own name servers.
How long a resolver may reuse a cached record before it must ask again.

stages.name: Going deeper
body: Not every answer is good news. If a name does not exist, the server says so, and that negative answer is cached too, so resolvers do not keep asking about a name that is not there. A negative answer has no record of its own to carry a time to live, so the server includes the zone's SOA record, and the cache time comes from that record [[rfc2308]].

A resolver normally has to trust whatever answer arrives. DNSSEC adds signatures to DNS data so a resolver can check that an answer really came from the zone's owner and was not changed on the way, including proof that a name does not exist [[rfc4033]]. Trust is chained from the parent: a parent zone publishes a DS record that vouches for the child zone's signing key.

DNSSEC has clear limits. It does not hide your queries, since DNS data is designed to be public, and it does not protect against floods of traffic meant to knock servers over [[rfc4033]]. It answers one question only: is this the data the zone's owner published?

terms.definition: The answer that a name does not exist.
Keeping a "does not exist" answer for a while, so the same question is not asked again and again.
The record at the top of a zone that describes it; it sets how long negative answers are cached.
Extensions that sign DNS data so resolvers can check where it came from and that it was not altered.
A record in the parent zone that vouches for a child zone's signing key.

stages.name: In practice and trade-offs
body: The root has to stay up for everyone, so each root server name is served by many machines in many places that share the same address. Network routing sends you to a nearby one, a technique called anycast. If one copy fails, traffic flows to another, and the list of root servers never has to change [[cs168]].

Caching is what makes DNS fast, and it is also what makes changes slow. A resolver keeps a record until its time to live runs out, so after you change a record, people can still get the old answer until their resolver's copy expires. A long time to live means fewer queries and steadier performance; a short one means changes are seen sooner but your servers answer more questions. Lowering it well before a planned change, then raising it again afterwards, is the usual compromise. This is common practice, not from a standard.

Most people use a recursive resolver chosen for them, by their internet provider or their network, and you can choose a different public one. Because resolvers serve many users, a popular answer is usually already cached, which is why most lookups finish without walking the tree at all [[cs168]].

terms.definition: Many servers in different places sharing one address, with routing sending each user to a nearby one.
The time it takes for a change to be seen everywhere, as cached copies expire.

misconceptions.myth: A DNS change takes effect everywhere at once.
misconceptions.truth: Resolvers keep cached copies until each copy's time to live runs out, so some people see the old answer for a while.

misconceptions.myth: The root servers know the address of every website.
misconceptions.truth: They only know which servers handle each top-level domain, and refer resolvers there [[bind-arm]].

misconceptions.myth: There are only 13 root server machines.
misconceptions.truth: There are 13 named root server authorities, served by hundreds of servers around the world [[iana-root]].
DNSSEC proves where data came from and that it was not changed; it does not hide what you look up [[rfc4033]].
